name: Chloe Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead carpenter for a rural builder in a market town, about fifteen of us, and we do oak-frame barns, garden rooms, farm sheds and repairs on old church roofs. At the moment I'm running the frame for an oak barn conversion, cutting the joints in our yard and then raising it on site with a crane and a lot of shouting. I start at seven with tea in the workshop, mark out the timbers, then it's chisels, a big chainsaw mortiser and pegging joints. I love raising day, when twenty tonnes of oak goes up and everything fits; what tires me out is the long drives between jobs and the mud in winter.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Daniel, my fiancé, on the edge of his family's dairy farm, in a cottage we rent from his parents. I sing in the church choir on Sundays, badly but loudly. I've used one of those AI chat things a few times, to check an old joint detail or help write a quote when the boss is away, but I don't use it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. We call it AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because you can't get a computer to feel how green oak moves. I'd say that at the pub, probably, and to the boss. I'm not much for online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means things carry on, and I'm glad. Our customers want old-fashioned craft, that's why they come to us. Daniel's farm goes on, my job goes on, we get married next spring as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, about four months put by. I'd probably use the AI a bit more for quotes and paperwork since it'd be proven by then. And I'd ask the boss again about taking on a girl from the college as an apprentice, because there's a keen one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite content. Like a good raising day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the apprentice from the college?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She reminds me of me at sixteen, always asking why. Somebody gave me a chance when lots of firms wouldn't take a girl, and I'd like to do the same. That's how a trade survives, one person passing it to the next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd worry about even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Maybe the farm, because milk prices are always a worry, but that's nothing to do with AI. That's just the weather and the supermarkets.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because no computer can feel how green oak moves. I'd say it at the pub and to the boss, not online.
S0.think: For me things carry on and I'm glad: our customers want old-fashioned craft. Daniel's farm goes on, my job goes on and we marry next spring as planned.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving, with about four months put by, and uses AI a bit more for quotes once it's proven. Asks her boss to take on a keen college student as an apprentice.
S0.feel: Calm and content, like a good raising day.
S0.quote: You can't get a computer to feel how green oak moves.
S0.fieldNote: Settled and rooted in craft, community and family farm life. Her one worry, milk prices, has nothing to do with AI. Passing the trade on to a young woman matters to her personally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the good firms will adapt, and people who are willing to work and learn will be fine. I'd say the government shouldn't get too involved, let firms and colleges sort the training. I'd say it at the pub, same as anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm mostly safe. Oak framing is a niche, and the people who pay for it want the hand-cut look. The machines might cut the rough joints, but someone still has to check them and raise the frame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what other oak-frame firms do, then I'd probably push my boss to get a CNC machine that cuts joints, once one was proven on oak. I'd learn to run it, maybe go on the manufacturer's course. And I'd use the AI for quoting and drawing more, now that everyone else is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit curious about the machines, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't a CNC take some of the craft out of your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, yes, and I'd be sad about that. But if it does the boring rough cuts, I get more time on the bits that matter, like the curved braces. My boss Martin's knees are going, he'd welcome anything that saves lifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lads who only do the rough stuff, cutting and stacking. They'd need to move up or move on. I'd want the firm to train them, not just let them go.

S1.say: I'd say good firms will adapt and people willing to work and learn will be fine. Government shouldn't get too involved; let firms and colleges sort the training.
S1.think: Off the record I'm mostly safe, since oak framing is a niche whose customers want the hand-cut look. Machines might cut rough joints, but someone still checks them and raises the frame.
S1.do: Waits to see how other oak-frame firms fare, then pushes her boss for a proven joint-cutting CNC machine and takes the manufacturer's course. Uses AI more for quoting and drawing.
S1.feel: Calm, with some curiosity about the machines.
S1.quote: But if it does the boring rough cuts, I get more time on the bits that matter, like the curved braces.
S1.fieldNote: Steady and practical: she'd adopt a machine once proven on oak. She wants firms rather than government to handle training. Her concern goes to the labourers doing rough work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's come far too fast and people weren't given a chance. I'd say families and churches will have to look after each other, because I don't trust the government to sort it in two years. I'd still say people should work wherever they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be very worried. If robots can raise an oak frame, then my niche is gone, and the farm might be automated too, so Daniel's family business changes. We'd be getting married with both our futures up in the air.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the wedding simple, the church and a barn do with home-cooked food, and keep the savings. I'd cut back on everything, sell my van and use the farm truck. I'd take whatever work was going in those two years and save as much as I could. And I'd lean on Daniel's family, because the farm at least gives us a roof and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the crane slipping with a beam in the air. My stomach drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the church. What would you say to people there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we look after each other, like we did when the floods came three years ago. People brought food round, helped clear houses. I think it would be like that, only bigger and longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to learn a new skill in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the machines, if there was a short course, so I could be the one who keeps them running locally. But honestly, two years, I'd be holding on. I'd learn whatever got us through.

S2.say: I'd say it came far too fast and people weren't given a chance, so families and churches will have to look after each other because I don't trust government to sort it in two years. People should still work wherever they can.
S2.think: Privately I'd be very worried: if robots can raise an oak frame my niche is gone, and Daniel's farm could be automated too. We'd marry with both futures up in the air.
S2.do: Keeps the wedding simple with a church service and a barn meal, sells her van and uses the farm truck, and saves all she can from any available work. Leans on Daniel's family farm for a roof and food.
S2.feel: Very worried, her stomach dropping like a crane slipping with a beam in the air.
S2.quote: I'd say we look after each other, like we did when the floods came three years ago.
S2.fieldNote: Her safety net is the farm, family and church, which she trusts over government. She worries for two livelihoods at once. Learning the machines is a thin hope; mostly she'd hold on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get ready, so let's get on with it. Apprenticeships in the new stuff, and firms that look after their people. I wouldn't want people waiting on handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years helps a lot. I'd have time to learn the machines properly and maybe set up something of my own on the side. I'd still be worried, but I'd have something to do with the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get the boss to buy the CNC and learn it properly. I'd also start making oak furniture from offcuts on weekends, benches and tables, and sell them at the farm shop, so there's a second bit of income. We'd marry as planned and keep renting the cottage instead of buying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious. I'd sleep alright most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would people still want hand-made furniture if robots make everything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would, I think, the way people still buy hand-thrown pots. Not many, mind. It's not a living, it's a top-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to set things up instead of just bracing for it. With two years, I'm clinging on. With five, I can start a little sideline and get the wedding done without panicking.

S3.say: I'd say we've got five years to get ready, so let's get on with it: apprenticeships in the new work and firms looking after their people, not handouts.
S3.think: Off the record, five years helps a lot: time to learn the machines and maybe start something of my own on the side. I'd still worry, but I'd have something to do with it.
S3.do: Gets her boss to buy a CNC and learns it properly in the first year. Starts making oak furniture from offcuts at weekends to sell at the farm shop, marries as planned and keeps renting instead of buying.
S3.feel: Anxious in a busy way, but sleeping alright most nights.
S3.quote: Some would, I think, the way people still buy hand-thrown pots. Not many, mind. It's not a living, it's a top-up.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her build a small sideline and learn the new machines. She is realistic that hand-made furniture is a top-up, not a living. The farm shop and rented cottage keep her plans grounded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of warning, and anyone who doesn't prepare only has themselves to blame. Firms and colleges should be training people now. And families should be getting their houses in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly settled. Ten years is long enough to build up the furniture business and maybe help Daniel's family modernise the farm. We'd have kids by then, and we'd make sure they had a trade and a bit of land behind them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the machines over the first couple of years, and grow the furniture side slowly, maybe a website by 2028. Daniel and I would marry, and at some point we'd probably put our savings into the farm, maybe a new barn or a farm shop extension. I'd keep a bit of money aside every month, always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, in the background. Mostly I'd feel I had time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone who doesn't prepare has themselves to blame. Isn't that harsh on people who can't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yes, you're right. Some folk are older or sick, and they'd need help from their families and the church. I meant people like me, young and fit, who've got no excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to learn, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade and how to look after land, and how to look after each other. Robots might do the work, but they won't sit with your gran when she's poorly. That's what I'd want them to know.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of warning, and anyone who doesn't prepare only has themselves to blame. Firms and colleges should train people now and families should get their houses in order.
S4.think: Privately I'd feel fairly settled: ten years is enough to build the furniture business and help Daniel's family modernise the farm. We'd have kids by then and give them a trade and some land behind them.
S4.do: Learns the joint-cutting machines over the first two years and grows the furniture business slowly, adding a website by 2028. Marries Daniel, later puts savings into the farm, such as a new barn or farm shop extension, and keeps saving monthly.
S4.feel: Slightly uneasy in the background but mostly feeling there's time.
S4.quote: Robots might do the work, but they won't sit with your gran when she's poorly.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, her plans centre on the farm, the furniture sideline and future children. When challenged on her harsh line about preparing, she softened it to young, fit people like herself. Family and faith remain her real safety net.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the farm and my job could go together. What would help is firms keeping people on and training them, and the community pulling together like after the floods. A bit of help for farms to adapt too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the countryside. Everyone talks about cities and offices, but out here if the farms and the builders go at once, the whole village goes quiet.

headlineQuote: If the farms and the builders go at once, the whole village goes quiet.
portrait: Chloe is a 27-year-old lead carpenter for a rural oak-frame builder, living with her fiancé Daniel on his family's dairy farm and singing in the church choir. She uses AI now and then and would adopt a joint-cutting machine once it was proven on oak. Calm in the plateau and in steady disruption, she becomes alarmed by fast AGI because her niche and the farm could go at once. With five or ten years she builds an oak furniture sideline, learns the machines and plans to invest in the farm. She trusts family, church and firms over government, softening her harsh line on people who don't prepare when challenged.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her job and Daniel's family farm could both go at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Firms keeping people on and training them, the community pulling together as it did after the floods, and some help for farms to adapt.
